Figure 1. Every protein of two animals, one tile each. Like Earth seen from space at night, lit tiles show where knowledge reaches, and ocean animals are the dark continents. The oyster has 10 times as many dark proteins as human (5,879 against 574). A match to a protein's own Swiss-Prot entry does not count. Hover or tap a tile to see the protein. Proteomes: UP000005640 and UP000005408, UniProt 2026_03, one protein per gene.

This site measures, for every software tool and every kind of organism, which proteins get a label and what the run costs, and tells each lab which tool to run. Today it scores 9 tools on human proteins. The first organism page will be the Pacific oyster's; it is not built yet, so there is no link to it.
Why ocean animals are dark
Science describes proteins where people work on them. Five species hold more reviewed proteins than all ocean animals put together, many times over.

Figure 2. The five best-studied species hold 90,318 reviewed proteins (15.7% of all), about 18,064 each. The 564 ocean animal species (the low end of Card 2) hold 2,702 together, 4.8 each on average. The other 11,201 species hold 482,669. 59 entries have no species and are left out. Human has 20,432 reviewed entries here; Figure 1 counts the 20,652 proteins of the human reference proteome, one per gene, reviewed or not. Source: Swiss-Prot, UniProt 2026_03 (02-Sep-2026); World Register of Marine Species habitat flags.
Mussel foot protein Mytilus edulis, Blue mussel, Q25460
Blue mussels use it to glue their threads to wet rock. Its repeated 10-residue stretches carry DOPA, a modified tyrosine, and chemists copy that chemistry to make glues that set under water.
A tool labels it today.

Antarctic rockcod make it to keep their blood from freezing in sea water below 0 °C. The chain is cut into 46 short glycopeptides, nearly all repeats of Ala-Ala-Thr, that stop ice crystals from growing.

Figure 3. Four ocean proteins that changed medicine and biology, and what the tools find on them today. Residues and features: UniProt 2026_03. Matches: the InterPro web service, and MMseqs2 against Swiss-Prot 2026_03.

The proteins that gave us underwater glue, antifreeze, a painkiller and the green light of cell biology were all found at the bench, by people, not by a tool. The three that tools label today are found by their likeness to proteins people described first; the antifreeze protein still gets no label. Three of the four are built from repeats or short peptides. On the leaderboard, the best tool finds 7 in 100 known features 2 to 15 residues long, against 28 in 100 features of any length. Repeats are found about as often as other features (30 in 100), and stretches with no fixed shape are not yet measured.

For scale: CAFA, the Critical Assessment of protein Function Annotation, has run as a community challenge since 2010. Open Problems (Luecken et al., Nature Biotechnology 2025, co-authored by Olga Botvinnik) does the same for single-cell analysis tools.
Who is behind it
Seanome Inc., a nonprofit.
The maintainers of nf-core/proteinannotator, the pipeline that labels a proteome's proteins.
If the proposed fork goes ahead (nothing agreed yet): the LAFA / CAFA group, who run functionbench.net (source).
Licence: the site's own repository has no licence file yet. Each tool keeps its own licence, listed on its tool card.
Contact: open an issue at github.com/seanome/protein-function-annotation-leaderboard/issues, or write to info@seanome.org.
